title: Pikelet - Breaking and Entering
summary: Lauren and Simon talk to Evelyn Ida Morris about the last Pikelet record, appropriately titled Goodbye.
transcript:
On 21 March 2019, Evelyn Ida Morris joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studio to discuss Goodbye, their final album as Pikelet, and a farewell show at the Church of All Nations in Carlton. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: We started with ‘Bug-In-Mouth’ from your self-titled debut in 2007, which was an Album of the Week here. I think it was when I pretty much first started presenting a regular show on Triple R. We just heard a new Pikelet track, ‘Plovers’. Welcome back.

Evelyn: I feel like this is my second home.

Simon: Over 12 years you’ve released five albums as Pikelet, one of which was shortlisted for the Australian Music Prize. You co-founded LISTEN, an advocacy group creating discourse around gender diversity and politics in Australian music. You had the self-titled release last year, and the ARIA-nominated soundtrack for Acute Misfortune.

Evelyn: I’m hoping that will come out as a proper release soon. The film premiered at MIFF last year and did really well, got some awards and things. All the reviews were very favourable in terms of my soundtrack. It was very exciting for me because I’ve wanted to do soundtrack music since I was a little kid. I was like, I’m going to be a concert pianist who wears tails on my coat, or a film soundtrack person. It feels really cool to have done my first feature. It’s funny now, letting go of Pikelet and doing Evelyn stuff. It feels like I’m growing up. It’s very fun, but I feel like I’ve always been growing up through music.

Simon: This Saturday you’re laying Pikelet to rest as a recording project. You’ve said you love ritual. Why is it important to mark the occasion in a ceremonial way?

Evelyn: There are so many reasons. I was raised with a pseudo-hippie upbringing, so I’ve always liked the idea of inventing my own rituals, finding ways to make certain moments feel special. Music does that anyway, but it’s also to do with my gender identity. Pikelet was very much a period of time where I was trying to perform femininity in this very heavy-handed way. I was never comfortable with that, so I would always overcomplicate the songs. I think you always are explaining a lot more than just what you’re saying in the songs when you’re doing these things. It feels good to let go of that attempt at an identity, and now to start to investigate what my identity is as a non-binary person. For other really huge, significant changes in people’s lives, like getting married, what other things do you have ceremonies for?

Simon: Initiations.

Evelyn: In some religious communities there are all sorts of rituals for growing older. Being someone who’s never really had much of an interest in religion, I thought it would be fun to mark this occasion in some way that feels ceremonious. We’re having some really beautiful flower arrangements made.

Lauren: Cecilia Fox, your friend?

Evelyn: Yeah, my friend Mel is going to make them. That’s really cool too, because I was just talking to her about it yesterday. She was front and centre at my very first Pikelet album launch, at a warehouse. It’s nice to reflect on that first album launch. I was so terrified and so unsure of what I was doing, and I feel very different about it this time. I still have to organise everything myself. I still do everything totally independently, and now I just am okay with that. Back then I was like, oh, I wish I was on a fancy huge label or whatever.

Simon: People attending this weekend will receive a little historical document, a pamphlet. Is that right?

Evelyn: Kind of. Actually, I shouldn’t talk it down. It’s a zine made by my friend Alice, and it’s going to have a little description of some of the things I’m feeling in terms of putting on this event. It’s also got photos from over the years by Lauren Bamford, who’s always been a good collaborator and a good friend. Everyone gets to take a little flower home. It’s beautiful, just a real dorky, fun thing. We’ve got some really nice natural wines to serve there as well. I tend to always like to, quote-unquote, pay the rent at gigs, donate to something current. This time there is the Djab Wurrung tree embassy situation going on. If you haven’t heard about it, please Google it and look up ways you can be supportive. You can call some politicians and donate money, because apparently they’re trying to make a decision about cutting down these really old trees that are very significant to some First Nations people. That decision is apparently being made Monday. Even though this action has been going on for a long time, now is quite a critical moment for it. I thought we would take a little money from the wine sales and other things and donate it, but also use it as a way to talk about it.

Lauren: Goodbye collects songs written in many locations over many years. Are there connecting threads you’re keen for people to understand?

Evelyn: The standard for me at the moment is non-binary visibility. I think it’s important to explore notions of gender identity in very in-depth ways. Mine is obviously just my version, and it’s a very therapeutic process for me to go through the song-making process and try to understand the shape of my gender. I also like presenting my version and being like, you’ll find your own version, whether people are cis or genderqueer or trans. It’s important for there to be an understanding that it’s always changing and always growing. That’s the main thread for these songs. One song in there is the first love song I’ve ever written, the first genuine lovey-dovey love song, which I always resisted doing when I was younger because I felt it was too feminine. I had this shame around femininity, and now I just feel it’s a lovely thing to celebrate being in love. When I was falling for my partner I was writing about that, but then it also started to become about knowing how to love my own processes and my own ups and downs in my mental health. It’s been a really celebratory process, this album, whereas the Evelyn Ida Morris album was very devo. It was like, this is what gender dysphoria feels like. There are a couple that are still like that, like a song called ‘Uterus’, which is pretty obvious. It’s been lovely collaborating with different filmmakers on clips. I made my first film clip myself, and I recorded this one myself. It feels very selfish, and I like that. If you’re not being true to your own self inside of your music, then why would you do it?

Simon: When you described the devastation at the heart of the Evelyn Morris debut album, there was also tremendous beauty. Was it a gift to yourself and others, encouraging people confused by a lack of certainty to embrace that?

Evelyn: That’s so nice that you noticed that. I feel like we’re all so very unaccustomed to feeling like it’s okay to be emotional, and it’s okay to be very sad, or it’s okay to be unsure and unclear. It’s nice to embrace that for myself, but I think it’s also important for other people to know they can. In some ways the most powerful and direct action of undermining the patriarchy is to express emotions and show them as a strength rather than something that’s supposed to be shameful or embarrassing. I’ve never been afraid of emotions, but in the Pikelet music I was definitely always being like, but also let’s put a happy spin on it. With that album I was like, you know what, actually things are pretty intense. I wrote the piano album just before starting LISTEN, so I was coming to terms with feminism and why it exists. It’s something I’m very proud of, even though I made a joke about it being devo. I’m really proud of it, and the next one’s almost done as well.

Lauren: How does the new Evelyn Ida Morris album relate to or differ from the album you released last year?

Evelyn: I’m always like a pendulum swinging between overdoing it, thinking too much about it and trying to prove something, and then letting things sit. That last Evelyn Morris album was very, look, I can play piano, I’m really good at it, I promise. Look how good I am. The next one is very meditative. It’s slow and has a lot of repetitive forms, a little bit of prepared piano and a lot more strings. I’m doing one song that’s a concept song, which I feel like I need a patent before I say it. I’m making a song with a repetitive form that’s pleasant to listen to, on piano and drums and some vibes. Then I’m explaining in spoken word my queer journey through high school, and how in high school often you learn how you’re supposed to hate your body. I’m going to release a version that has no speaking on it so other people can put their own version on it. It’s a daggy idea, but I’m really into it because it makes me feel better about that feeling of, my journey is not the only journey.

Lauren: Sharing your own experience so it may help others as well.

Evelyn: Yeah, and also making a space for other people to express theirs, if they wanted to.

Simon: Like karaoke for feelings.

Lauren: The Pikelet farewell show is this Saturday, 23 March, at the Church of All Nations in Carlton. You’ve been asking people to share their Pikelet memories. Is that still happening?

Evelyn: Kind of. I’m just excited to be able to have a moment to reflect with other people who have enjoyed it. There’s this tendency in a lot of music circles where we feel like we have to be like, oh, that was dumb, I didn’t like it, I did it ages ago and it’s stupid now, always moving forward. It’s nice to have a little nostalgia as well. It’s crazy to me that it’s been over 10 years. It’s so weird. When I heard you play the song from the first album in the car, I was like, oh my gosh, who is this person?

Simon: What are your plans for Sunday, the day after the ceremonial Pikelet farewell?

Evelyn: Probably not very much. I’ll probably go for a walk, go to the park with my partner and my dog, sleep a lot and eat some nice food. I think that’s it. It’ll be a nice relief. Then I’ve got a bunch of plans coming up to go to the States because this album’s come out on a small label in LA called Babyrace.

Simon: Shout out to Shags Chamberlain.

Evelyn: Yeah, Shags Chamberlain and Joe McKee are the two expat Aussies that started that label. I’m going to get to go and have a trip over there, which is cool. It’s exciting.
